speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But we need to continually review and update this piece of legislation as our City in a Garden continues to transform and grow.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The Marine Park was established in 2014, after many years of hard work by NParks colleagues and passionate members of our marine conservation community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: They include representatives from the Nature Society Singapore, Wild Singapore, the academic community and many other committed individuals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In particular, I would like to thank Mr Francis Lee, the lead for the Blue Plan, Prof Chou Loke Ming, a luminary in the field of marine biology, Mr Leong Kwok Peng, Vice President of Nature Society Singapore and Ms Ria Tan, Singapore's passionate naturalist and many, many more.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The coastal areas and waters in the Marine Park teem with life and are rich in local biodiversity, such as coral, anemones, seahorses, fish and other creatures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It is amazing that our waters, which lie within some of the busiest commercial sea lanes in the world, are home to over a third of the world's total coral species.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, protecting the reefs at the Sisters' Island Marine Park is crucial to our coral conservation efforts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For instance, it will be an offence to fish, collect corals or moor boats without NParks' approval.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The Bill will also enable NParks to make new subsidiary rules to regulate human activities in the Marine Park, in order to keep it as a sanctuary for marine life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For example, NParks can restrict diving and dropping of anchors at ecologically sensitive Let me next move on to provisions that enhance protection of biodiversity in our nature reserves.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Section 9(3)(a) of the Act restricts the bringing in or releasing of animals in a nature reserve.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This prevents the introduction of invasive species which may threaten the survival of our native animals in the reserves.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: To make this clear, NParks will put up signage at key watercourses and continue to strengthen its public education efforts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Third, the Bill gives greater protection to public parks and gardens that are not managed by NParks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Gardens by the Bay is independently managed by Gardens by the Bay Company (GB Co).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Clause 4 of the Bill now allows the Minister to designate entities like GB Co as managers of public parks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Clause 2(d) also brings these parks under the protection of the Parks and Trees Act, while clause 3(b) further allows the Commissioner of Parks and Recreation to delegate certain enforcement powers to selected employees of these entities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In short, GB Co employees can now rely on the Parks and Trees Act's provisions to protect the greenery and biodiversity of Gardens by the Bay.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For example, park wardens who are GB Co employees will now be able to take enforcement action against illegal cutting of trees and plants at Gardens by the Bay.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Fourth, the Bill provides NParks with more effective regulatory and enforcement powers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Under clause 3, the Commissioner of Parks and Recreation may delegate certain powers of enforcement to public officers, NParks employees, as well as the Auxiliary Police officers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: He can also appoint public officers, NParks employees, an employee of a management body designated under section 6A, as well as licensed security officers as park rangers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: These officers will receive proper enforcement training and work closely with NParks officers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In addition, NParks officers will now have more effective powers to investigate offences under the Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For instance, they may interview offenders and record statements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Fifth, the Bill empowers NParks to require greenery to be reinstated, in cases where it has been illegally removed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Currently, when greenery along Heritage Road green buffers are removed, offenders will not only face a fine, they may also be ordered to reinstate the greenery.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: However, those who commit illegal tree-felling in Tree Conservation Areas and vacant land are currently only subject to fines.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This brings the regulatory treatment for both Heritage Road green buffers as well as Tree Conservation Areas into alignment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Sixth, the Bill enhances public safety by ensuring that occupiers of private property maintain the greenery in their premises.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This includes trees grown on roof tops and balcony gardens.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: These trees need to be properly maintained or they might constitute a danger to occupiers and bystanders alike.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Clause 14 will also allow NParks officers to enter premises to ascertain the condition of trees and plants to safeguard public safety.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Maintenance notices may be issued to occupiers if the trees or plants pose a danger to persons or property.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: These notices may require the occupier to engage an arborist to conduct detailed inspections or to carry out pruning.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: These powers will only be exercised as a last resort, if the occupier is uncooperative.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Seventh, the Bill restructures the Parks and Trees Act to better enable NParks to respond more quickly and dynamically to new trends in greenery development.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Presently, very technical specifications, such as the dimensions of planting areas that surround buildings, are set out in the Parks and Trees Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: These requirements cannot be modified or waived even by the Commissioner of Parks and Recreation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This industry, comprising landscape designers, maintenance workers, arborists and nursery operators, is crucial to the development and maintenance of our City in a Garden.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Since 2007, NParks has rolled out industry training programmes and best practice guides.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In 2016, NParks worked with NTUC and MOM to launch a Progressive Wage Model for landscape workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In this regard, clause 24 defines the landscape industry and NParks' role in helping to manage, promote and strengthen the industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: They underscore our determination to ensure that our greenery and natural heritage will endure.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The campaign to green Singapore has, indeed, been very successful and despite the demand for housing and other infrastructure we are indeed maintaining our image as a garden city.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, the success of our policy has also brought on some ugly issues between neighbours in some private estates.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The recent case highlighted in the media between two private homeowners is an example.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I have received feedback from residents who complained that their neighbours did not maintain their trees properly and, as a result, the trees are leaning over, or the leaves fall into their garden, or the roots are uprooting the boundary wall.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: These residents are at a dilemma because not all neighbours are so understanding and cooperative.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They view that as long as it is on their land, they can do what they want.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The overgrown trees may tilt or drop leaves into the next house but it is not their problem.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: For the ones at the receiving end, there is no redress.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There is no one that they can turn to.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Do not ask them to go for mediation as they will not turn up and do not ask them to go and look for the neighbourhood committee members because neighbourhood committee can keep knocking at the door, they would not open the door.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Of course, if there is a danger of human lives, then this amendment would be helpful as NParks can now step in.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Is the dropping of leaves into the neighbour's house that may clog up drains and cause mosquito breeding and dengue or Zika a danger?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Or the leaves fall into the neighbour's house cause the neighbour to have sleepless nights and subsequently have depression − is this danger?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Since there is already a lot of roadside planting, can NParks order to remove trees that cause dispute or concern?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   Many residents in private estates would tell me that their neighbour's tree was "leaning over".

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: As a result, the leaves would fall into their garden, or the tree looked so precarious that they would feel afraid every day.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If the Neighbourhood Committee was asked to mediate, their neighbour may even refuse to answer the door!

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is because there are a lot of trees and flowers planted along the roadside.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In English): Mdm Speaker, these clarifications notwithstanding, I support the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The objective to protect Singapore's coral reefs, which are home to rare and endangered marine life, is lofty and praiseworthy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The plans for the marine park to serve as a platform for conservation, research, outreach and education on our marine biodiversity are ambitious and worthy of support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We will be protecting what is leftover of our natural heritage after the incessant urban development and redevelopment, not for ourselves, but for our children and for the world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the face of warming waters of climate change, protecting our tiny coral reefs is a statement of defiant sustainability.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a shout-out to everyone that we need to conserve our common future, no matter how small the contribution and how slim the chances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is also a promising social aspect leading to the establishment of the marine park.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It was born from the proposal by civil society called the Singapore Blue Plan 2009.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Various local NGOs and institutions worked with NParks during the International Year of the Reef in 2008 to develop the Plan, which was submitted to the Government.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As a result, the Comprehensive Marine Biodiversity Survey was launched, led by NParks and involved the Universities, many NGOs and many more volunteers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government's move to establish the marine park is a ringing endorsement of civil society's initiative.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It shows what non-governmental organisations and social clubs can achieve by pooling their creative energies and what can be accomplished for the national good when the Government listens and allows the creative energies to be channelled through to policy and law.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have been looking forward to this Bill to formalise the legal status of the marine park and I am disappointed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Both disappointments are related to the objective of protecting our coral reefs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first is the scope of protection and the second is the scale of protection.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let us begin with the scope of protection.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Bill defines "marine park" as "any area of the sea or seabed that is set aside for conservation of marine organisms and is designated in Part III of the Schedule".

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So far so good, as the marine park seems to take on the characteristics of "national park" and "nature reserve", being set aside for conservation and designated with its own Part in the Schedule.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the "marine park" is then parked, forgive the pun, under the definition of "public park".

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are two national parks: Fort Canning Park and the UNESCO World Heritage-listed Singapore Botanic Gardens.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And there are four nature reserves: the Central Catchment Nature Reserve, Bukit Timah Nature Reserve, Labrador Nature Reserve and Sungei Buloh Wetland Reserve.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These areas are set aside for conservation of our natural heritage, scientific research, outreach and dissemination of knowledge and educational purposes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These are exactly aligned with the purposes of the marine park, to serve as a platform for conservation, research, outreach and education on our marine biodiversity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, why is our only and very unique marine park not placed with our national parks and nature reserves, but lumped with over 300 public parks?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is not just a question of bad categorisation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The protections that are afforded to national parks and nature reserves should be given to our marine park, for the simple reason that our marine park was established to protect our unique and endangered marine biodiversity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I understand that in any nature conservation effort, outreach and education are important to get public support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The intertidal walks, the trails, the planned boardwalk and the floating pontoon at Big Sister's Island complement the conservation effort.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, they do expose the fragile marine eco-system to human footfalls and the natural temptation to touch and collect.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Furthermore, as a public park, the marine park is exposed to visitors in private boats who could swim and snorkel freely among the reefs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Designating the marine park as a nature reserve, and not just any public park, will signal to visitors to give due respect to the marine biodiversity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is one more reason why the marine park needs the protection of a nature reserve, even more so than a terrestrial nature reserve.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The boundaries of a terrestrial nature reserve, such as Sungei Buloh, could be carefully guarded against human intrusions using well-designed fences, walls, roads, hedges, waterways or secondary forests.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the marine park is by nature a very open space given its location in the open seas.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As our marine park gathers fame, our marine biodiversity could become a target of unscrupulous poachers and collectors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One major threat to coral reefs and reef fishes is poaching for the aquarium hobby market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to empower the custodian, NParks, to guard the marine park against this threat.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Blue Plan had a far more extensive list of areas with high marine biodiversity, which included many islands and reefs adjacent to the marine park, such as Pulau Hantu, Pulau Semakau, Pulau Biola, the Cyrene Reefs and Kusu Island.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Expanding the marine park to cover these areas with submerged reefs would greatly enhance and deepen the protection of our marine biodiversity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Kusu Island is also a cherished place for thousands of Singaporeans travelling there for religious pilgrimages.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The legend behind the island about a tortoise turning itself into an island to save two shipwrecked sailors, a Malay and a Chinese, and the Chinese temple and kramat shrines located there represent our multiracial harmony.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Kusu Island presents us with the opportunity to integrate an area of cultural significance into the marine park, to enhance it as a place of natural and cultural heritage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is also the need to create buffer zones in between the conserved areas.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Unrestricted shipping poses a threat to the separated pockets of marine biodiversity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Buffer zones providing for secondary protection, not unlike the proposed amendment to create a new offence of releasing animals into a reserve through waterways outside the reserve, would mitigate the risks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am fully aware that the shipping traffic is the lifeline of our economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the relocation of the port from Keppel and Pasir Panjang to Tuas presents us with an excellent opportunity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The URA has invited Singaporeans to imagine and envision how the planned redevelopment of the coastline for the Greater Southern Waterfront after 2030 can take shape.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe we should not stop at the creation of a continuous waterfront from Labrador to Marina South and we should creatively and courageously imagine the inclusion of an expanded Southern Islands Marine Park as the Greater Southern Waterfront's premium green space.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Instead of limiting the green network to the corridor from Labrador Park and Mount Faber to Pulau Brani, we should think outside the terrestrial green box to a great national park that integrates Labrador Nature Reserve and its green corridor with the blue network of coral reefs of the Southern Islands.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have a third point to add to the two disappointments concerning the scope and scale of protecting our marine biodiversity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This third point is the fear the amendments in this Bill will shift the evolution of the marine park in an undesirable direction.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will this lead to the commercialisation of our public parks?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will this lead to the parcelling out of our 300-plus public parks to diverse organisations to turn them into spaces to carry out their agenda that may undermine or dilute the open character and recreational purpose of our public parks?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will this promote unhealthy competition and turf wars between entities, such as Residents Committees, non-profit groups and even Statutory Boards?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope the Senior Minister of State will clarify the intention of this amendment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a dangerous proposition, as the marine park needs to be managed by an entity equipped with the right scientific and conservation expertise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: NParks is the only entity that is properly equipped to manage the marine park.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Reading the two amendments together, defining the marine park as a public park and allowing other entities to manage public parks, I fear that the marine park will be taken down the road to become an eco-tourist theme park one day.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will definitely subvert the aim of conserving our marine biodiversity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope the Senior Minister of State can state, categorically, that this is not the direction it will take the marine park towards.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The marine park represents to us our hope for the future, the legacies we leave behind for our children, an unrivalled lesson in good stewardship and the values we cherish as a cosmopolitan island nation embracing the world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should deepen the scope and expand the scale of protecting our marine biodiversity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should not turn what should be a nature reserve into an eco-tourist theme park.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Can I get clarification on the definition of this threat to life and property?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Some of the issues that we tend we face on the ground may include trees bearing fruits which drop and accidentally hit persons or even vehicles parked in the vicinity, to cracks and damages to paths and pavements due to the expanding root systems.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Some clarification will be useful as this is a practical problem.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Therefore, it will be good to also have some idea on the timeline for pruning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Barring all these, Madam, I will support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have no objections to the Bill, but I would like to speak about gaps in our current regime for managing trees and parks, as well as to raise some technical questions about certain provisions in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In November last year, I asked the Minister for National Development what are the criteria that NParks uses to make decisions about tree-cutting, and/or replanting activities in residential estates, whether these criteria vary according to the location and nature of the residential estate and, if so, how?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And how are residents consulted in the process?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If it is deemed necessary by NParks' arborists or contractors, NParks will then study replanting options and make a decision about what replacement trees to plant, based on technical considerations like available space, presumably soil condition, sunlight exposure at that location and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The reply also said, "Residents are consulted when there is an opportunity to rejuvenate the overall landscaping of the estate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, NParks seeks feedback on landscaping options and tree-planting schemes as part of the estate upgrading programme and for large projects, such as Jurong Lake Gardens".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The reply did not state if there was a process for consulting residents about decisions on replacing groups of trees near residential estates, or planting new clusters, in other words, for tree planting decisions that are not related to big projects.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I can only assume that no such structured and regular process exist.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, one family living in a landed estate where trees line the path from the market to the house − and this is a group of people who clearly have a strong interest in flora, and in plants and trees, and have a great deal of knowledge about that subject − they shared with me that the group of trees that they had loved and which had afforded them good shade on hot days, had been replaced by a tree species which was less shady.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I note that this wish to have some say over the types of trees planted in a particular area is also felt by some residents in the HDB estate where I live.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some might argue that this is a trivial matter over which to have a consultation process.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some might argue that a matter such as this does not warrant such consultation and that it might overburden NParks to build this into NParks' regular procedures.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, efficient solutions can be found that do not stretch the resources in manpower of NParks to conduct such consultations, and this solution can be deployed only when there is significant new planting or replanting, and not for the replacement of just a single tree.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Residents could submit a very simple online form with their NRIC to express support for one or another option.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The residents could learn about the page through noticeboards in HDB estates, or by signboards placed strategically at landed estates.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One could argue against this by saying that if only certain people go online and express a preference, then the decision will be undemocratic.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, that is still better than no one being given a chance to express a preference.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Moreover, more votes may be generated by individual residents urging their neighbours to go online and vote for their preferred option.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It could be argued that this is giving residents too much choice NParks could provide only certain options for tree choice based on local considerations, such as soil considerations and so on, and also based on national considerations, like the need to preserve a certain level of biodiversity in the national tree population which has broader ecological benefits for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In fact, if such a model of consultation can be piloted and run efficiently, it could serve as an inspiration for local consultation and empowerment on other matters that fall into the middle zone, where they are neither too big to warrant a formal vote, nor too small to ignore residents' feedback altogether.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have suggested an online approach to consultation because this would seem to be efficient and scalable, but there could be other approaches to achieve the same result, bearing in mind that many Singaporeans are still not too IT-savvy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such exercises could inspire a greater sense of ownership over the local greenery and public park spaces.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This, in turn, could enhance positive behaviours like anti-littering and that could have a knock-on effect of saving state expenditure in other areas.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such consultations could even stimulate interaction among residents as they lobby one another for their own preferred treescapes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Lastly, such exercises could stimulate a better understanding and appreciation of the beauty of our natural flora in Singapore, as well as of the work of NParks.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In past decades, there have been residential developments constructed at the margins of the Central Catchment in Bukit Timah Nature Reserves.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These incidents may disrupt the reserves' delicate eco-system and biodiversity.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What measures are in place now or will be considered in the future to limit these possibilities, or limit the damage that might be caused from such possibilities?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Conversely, what happens when animals accidentally exit the reserves and are found by residents in these developments who may decide to capture and retain the animals, or even harm them?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They should by right call NParks to return animals that are captured, but, if they do not, what recourse does NParks have in such cases?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, I have a few questions that are more technical in nature.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Clause 3b of the Bill also now I think this is a matter of public interest because if, for example, there has been a rise in offences that warrant this, it is a matter of public interest to understand what these offences are.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, if there has been a spike in incidents of persons harming or poaching endangered species of animals or plants in our nature reserves, many concerned citizens and NGOs may want to know about this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I ask this because I wonder if we have given due considerations in other ways to minimise offences occurring on NParks' land, such as CCTV cameras or apps that allow members of the public to photograph and report offences that they see.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is a similar sight that greets Singaporeans returning home.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Since 1975, when the Parks and Trees Act replaced the then Botanical Gardens Act, the NParks has worked hard to ensure that this continues to grow from the vision of our founding Prime Minister, Mr Lee Kuan Yew of having a "Garden City" or a "City within a Garden".

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Much of this is in the past is in fulfilment of benign religious beliefs or personal obligations, but at the malicious end, also because of cruelty.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For the existing fauna in our waterways, the introduction of new, perhaps invasive life could prove to be a major disruption.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There is a real problem of having invasive aquatic species released into our nature reserves or other water sources leading to it.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In the United States, the problem of predatory and large snakeheads is well documented.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In Asia, perhaps our solution is to make them into soup but in the US, it is a major problem.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The population of this invasive fish has grown at such a prolific rate that there have been reports of snakeheads, which can survive outside of water for a period of time, walking and crossing between waterways and even, anecdotally, having been reported of attacking humans!

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Singapore has thrived and prided itself in avoiding black swan situations.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This legislation that we have and are debating on at this moment would go further in correcting the threats to our biodiversity by imported fauna.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Improper control can lead to the spread of bacterial diseases as well, which could wipe out our marine life in our nature parks and adjoining waterways.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The potential for negative environmental impact is there and it is only proper that laws are tightened to ensure that our existing flora and fauna are protected.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In fact, even from a religious standpoint, major religious organisations have come together with NParks in the annual Operation No Release to encourage Singaporeans and clarify that the releasing of live animals is not to be encouraged if it causes greater suffering.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To quote Mr Henry Baey, then-President of the Buddhist Fellowship, who said in 2010, "Compassion and wisdom are like two wings on the same bird.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One without the other is only futile, it can even be dangerous.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Releasing animals may seem like a beautiful, kind, meritorious thing to do.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, if it upsets the ecosystem and causes harm, not only to the animals released, but to all living creatures in the area, can that then be called a genuine act of compassion?" Operation No Release has been in effect for a number of years and I understand that the number of cases in our nature reserves and our waterways has gone down.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But the problem seems to have moved proverbially upstream to other waterways and canals that people may not be aware will lead into our nature reserves.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But being a city that is very prone to rain and a very large network of drains and canals, perhaps what is more important is further education and public communications.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I welcome the added protection for trees, especially in private estates and in private property, but I wish to clarify a point in clauses 14 and 18.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yesterday, we debated and passed the Planning (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The hon Member for Nee Soon Er Dr Lee Bee Wah, in her clarification, had asked if URA, the lead agency for the Planning Bill, could be empowered to ensure that issues, such as plastering works, could be done.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, the explanation provided yesterday was that homeowners will need to have their premises and privacy respected.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I accept the explanation by the Senior Minister of State earlier that this would be the last resort.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, I wish to ask if there is a slight disjoint in the implementation between these two different Bills.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One where NParks public officers are allowed to enter and to make corrections whereas another agency, under the same Ministry, is not allowed to do so.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Because at the end of the day, while a tree may fall and cause danger to the public, a non-plastered wall after some time of exposure can also potentially cause danger to the public as well.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is a move in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Singapore, over the years, is not known for being very diverse in our marine life, but it is, and this designation of the marine park is a step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In my constituency of Yew Tee, we are blessed to have the Sungei Buloh Wetlands Reserve and the Kranji Marshes at our doorstep.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I understand that the Prime Minister came to jalan jalan at the Marshes last Sunday as well.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These 50-plus hectares of protected marshes full of flora and an abundance of fauna is worth protecting.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But I have a question for the Senior Minister of State because there is cause for concern amongst nature lovers as major developments across the straits, in fact at the mouth of the straits, have long-term detrimental impact on the reserve.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: My last point is in relation to clause 24 under the powers given to NParks.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The new functions empower NParks to manage on behalf of the Government any state land used by the landscape industry.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Then-Prime Minister Mr Lee Kuan Yew envisioned Singapore to be a highly liveable city-state that not only provided economic opportunities to her residents, but would also have a high quality of life.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: People would be able to live in a beautiful environment where roads were tree-lined and parks and green open spaces were freely accessible to everyone.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Over the years, NParks has spearheaded the development of new parks and green recreational spaces.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It has also continued to promote and develop research in botany, environmental biology and forestry management.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To continue this work, I believe it is necessary to strengthen NParks' regulatory function and power and would thus like to speak on three specific amendments of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First of all, the designation of "marine park" as a type of "public park".

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As we have already heard from Senior Minister of State Desmond Lee, the Straits of Singapore is one of the busiest commercial shipping routes in the world.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In spite of this busy maritime traffic, the Straits has a remarkably diverse marine life.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some of the marine animals spotted in the Straits of Singapore include the Hawksbill Turtle, the Indo-Pacific Humpbacked Dolphin and Black-tipped Reef sharks.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On a more positive note, having greater regulatory and enforcement power may potentially allow Singapore to capitalise on our rich marine biodiversity to promote marine tourism and other marine leisure activities.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Popular Singapore sites, such as Pulau Hantu, are overused and there are signs of coral damage.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The designation of "marine parks" as "public parks" will thus potentially offer NParks a clearer channel to develop other dive sites, possibly in our southern waters.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While Singapore can never realistically compete with a place like the Maldives for marine tourism, it could be fruitful for NParks to work with operators to enhance more sea-sport and marine leisure offerings to feed domestic demand.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, a well-conserved marine park would also offer educational opportunities, especially for our youth, on the bio-riches of our waters and the importance of sustainable living.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would, however, also like to suggest that NParks eventually oversee the management of all trees and plants across the island.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that such a move will resolve the current slightly complex management system of trees and plants that is in place.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the present moment, depending on the configuration and location, you could have trees and plants in the area of a few hundred square metres coming under the jurisdiction and management of various diverse agencies, such as LTA, HDB, NParks and the Town Councils.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While the public can call the MSO line to deal with any issue pertaining to the trees and plants concerned and their feedback will be re-routed to the appropriate agency, I feel that this might not be the most efficient and cost-effective way to address such concerns.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Under the current system, I understand that each individual agency will need to call for its own tender for horticultural contracts and maintain its own horticultural team, even arborist, to deal with such exigencies and issues.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This, potentially, leads to the duplication of contracts and manpower across agencies when what is needed is perhaps a singularly-managed horticultural team and a few master contracts that cover the maintenance of plants and trees across the island In my opinion, it would thus be more prudent and effective, from both a resource and manpower standpoint, to have NParks to be the lead coordinating agency that oversees the entire process of maintaining all our trees and plants in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The complaints are about how insects and birds nesting in those trees are a nuisance and disturbance.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Specifically, insects are flying into their homes and birds are defecating in their balconies.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our community leaders have raised the matter but little has been done to alleviate the situation so far.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This would potentially help to alleviate the situation I have just highlighted, as well as other similar situations that I am sure my parliamentary colleagues would face, as those responsible for the trees will now have to comply with maintenance notices issued by NParks.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am glad that these issues will be given due attention.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On the other hand, I am also concerned about the technical interpretation of the proposed changes and whether these changes will lead to frequent situations where various parties expect NParks to step in to resolve minor issues that could be dealt with in other ways and using other channels.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, how else could the concept of "danger" be applied?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With that, Mdm Speaker, I conclude my speech in support of the Bill and look forward to NParks continuing to integrate more biodiversity and flora into our urban landscape, so that we are not only a Garden City but a City in a Garden.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.20 pm.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Prolific urban planning has led to a boom of construction projects around Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some of these projects would involve the removal and transplanting of trees.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I understand that NParks takes a keen interest in heritage trees, as well as tree removal and transplantation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Extensive consultations would take place between the project management team of the construction projects and NParks with regard to these matters.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, I have received feedback from residents in my constituency that the trees in the vicinity of construction works are sometimes not cared for properly by the respective construction teams, or are even damaged.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Examples include improper trimming and pruning, as well as defacement of trees.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Next, having a beautiful garden is an aspect that many landed property owners enjoy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And it is good that they would like to maintain a garden at their own expense, considering that it means additional green spaces as well as fresher air in the neighbourhood.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, some property owners lack consideration for their neighbours and, as a result, common disputes among neighbours living in the private property estates often involve inappropriate placement of trees.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, in cases where there is a clear violation of regulations stipulated by MND, would it not be more appropriate for someone, such as NParks, to intervene?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I would imagine that the regulations are in place for good reasons, mostly safety-related, and it would make more sense to deal with it as soon as possible, rather than using authoritative power as a last resort.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: NParks' focus has been on trees but I believe they also look into other plants and assess how they affect the public.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some plants like cacti are top favourites in landscaping works because they are hardy and aesthetically pleasing.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, some species can grow very big and may cause safety hazards and obstruction.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If a resident notices potential issues arising from a non-tree type of plant, can NParks be called upon for assistance?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Last but not least, many landed property owners hire private grass-cutters and tree-cutters to tend their garden.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some of these grass-cutters or tree-cutters come and do the work on a lovely Sunday morning and disrupt the peace with noise from their machines when most residents would have liked to enjoy a peaceful morning jog or stroll, or even sleep in.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Their noise level goes up as high as 100 decibels and then sometimes lasts half an hour or more.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This exceeds the stipulated safety restrictions by MOM, which dictates that, for the safety of workers, exposure to 100 decibels should not exceed 15 minutes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Fortunately for the workers, they may wear hearing protectors which allow them to safely do their work at high noise levels.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But what about the residents who do not have these hearing protectors?

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Mr Henry Kwek is not in the House.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have spent the last 16 years of my life fighting to protect our wildlife here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: With ACRES, we have rescued thousands of animals, rehabilitated them and, working with both NParks and AVA, released them back into the wild where they belong.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Singaporeans continue to be amazed when I tell them that we rescued over 1,000 wild animals in Singapore each year.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: ACRES alone rescued more than 3,000 wild animals just last year.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The most common response I get is "Singapore got wild animals, meh?" I have personally seen the amazing biodiversity we have on this island, I have seen how precious they are and, perhaps most importantly, I have seen how fragile they are.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have much to lose if our policies are not right and, for all the harm that we humans have done to the animals and the environment, it is also only us who can right this wrong; only us who can protect our ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A significant step forward is in the protection of our marine ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If it is hard to create awareness of and protect the biodiversity on land, protect our terrestrial ecosystem, then it is even harder when it comes to our marine ecosystem simply because what goes on there literally goes on beneath the surface and most people have never seen or heard of the amazing marine life we have in our waters.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There should be an equivalent to Part III of the PTA with regard to marine parks.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There should be a section setting out the objectives of a marine park, similar to section 7 of the current Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There should also be provisions setting out what acts are prohibited in a marine park, similar to sections 8 and 9 of the current Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What is the status of the land areas of Sisters Island?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is only the marine area, defined in the Bill's Schedule Part III, that is protected as a marine park.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But the amended It is noted as well that shellfish is protected, as "fish" includes shellfish in the definition.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But this protection only applies to acts that are prohibited in sections 8 and 9 and these relate to National Parks and Nature Reserves, not to a marine park.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify if the protection extends to the marine park as well?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What about shells that no longer have shellfish living in them, the giant clam shells, for example?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There was a recent controversy over the giant clam shells collected by NUS students on a trip to the Riau Islands.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is also unclear if corals are protected in a marine park.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It may be argued that the definition of "animal" in the PTA is wide enough to encompass corals "or any other living creature, vertebrate or invertebrate".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While many are living organisms, some corals may be dead.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Section 14 of the State Lands Encroachment Act makes it an offence to take "corals or shells" from state land but this only applies to taking from the "land".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Is this to be considered "land" as well?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is best if the law clearly makes it an offence to take away shellfish, shells as well as corals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: All these should be protected in a marine park, along with fish and other marine creatures.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is also unclear if fishing or the taking of any marine life in a marine park is prohibited.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will there also be prohibitions on throwing down of anchors onto the seabed as these would damage the coral reefs, or throwing of garbage into the sea?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I appreciate that the Minister had mentioned earlier that there would be subsidiary legislation enacted that will probably address a majority of the concerns I have raised but I hope again that as we draft those regulations, the points I raise here are taken into consideration.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The experience with the designation of "Chek Jawa Wetlands" in 2007 suggests that amendments to the PTA are necessary to allow NParks to fully enforce the PTA beyond the high water mark.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand from the green community that NParks Notice 5.2.180.1 dated 24 September 2007 and Port Marine Notice No 126 of 2007 attempted to designate Chek Jawa Wetlands by demarcating points in the sea and declaring via the Notices that these points were under the PTA.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Probably because there was no actual corresponding amendments to the PTA, in practice, even after the Notices, NParks still has to send all reported misdemeanours beyond the high water mark to MPA to enforce.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: NParks could not enforce action on its own against blatant misbehaviour in broad daylight within the designated Chek Jawa Wetlands.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These include laying fish nets These experiences underline the importance of embedding clear jurisdiction boundaries in the sea through amendments in the PTA, and not just via Notices.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this light, could the Ministry also look at amending jurisdiction for coastal parks, nature reserves and Chek Jawa, since it is now amending jurisdiction for the Sisters Islands marine park?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, on the amendments to section 9, which propose to prohibit the release or abandonment of animals into any river, stream or watercourse which flows into a nature reserve.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that NParks will be putting up "no-release" signs to inform the public of this change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, it might be difficult to enforce this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For example, if the public releases the animal further upstream, before the sign is sighted, how will this law still be enforced?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How will we assess if the person "reasonably knows" that the body of water flows into or through the nature reserve?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A person caught releasing the animal can simply say he or she does not know the river flows into the nature reserve.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: ACRES has seen first-hand the devastating impact invasive species can have on local ones.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I had the privilege of experiencing the amazing biodiversity in Singapore and I hope my daughters will continue to have this privilege when they are older.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I was in England recently and I watched a programme on TV about the challenges countries around the world faced in co-existing with their wild animals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The programme ended by showcasing Singapore and how we have succeeded in protecting our biodiversity and co-existing with our wild animals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The ball is in our court and let us make sure we do what is right.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: After all, "If we pollute the air, water and soil that keep us alive and well, and destroy the biodiversity that allows natural systems to function, no amount of money will save us." Madam, I stand in full support of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Today, as we debate on the amendments, I would like to talk about the broader point, which is to deepen the connection between our people and our nature.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: It means that Nature's beauty brings forth talent and character in people.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Indeed, for those of us who have experienced the joy of nature, we know intuitively that nature centres and nourishes the soul.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, most Singaporeans I meet hold NParks in high regard.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In particular, my residents appreciate how NParks has tended to Bishan Park and Lower Pierce Reservoir Park, as well as the numerous neighbourhood parks nestled within Kebun Baru.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: My residents are also looking forward to the upcoming Upper Thomson Nature Park sited next to the Central Reserve.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Given the significant efforts we have invested in ensuring that nature is at our people's doorstep, we should strive to get as many Singaporeans to walk through that door and to enjoy the full extent of Singapore's beautiful nature.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: NParks has done an excellent job to engage the public.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Just to name a few, over the last year, NParks has done a comprehensive programme for interested schools and preschools to partake in developing apps, such as the SG BioAtlas, to help Singaporeans share and identify distinctive Singaporean plants and animals that they have spotted.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But while NParks is working hard to engage Singaporeans, it is going against the prevailing trend where our children and youths are growing up as fully-fledged digital natives and emotionally disengaging from the physical world.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Increasingly, mobile phones and iPads are becoming digital pacifiers for our children.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We see that at every coffee shop, at every social gathering and pretty much in every home with young children.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This trend is not just limited to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Last year, my wife and I hiked at a National Park in the United States for two days.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We were surprised to encounter a slick advertising blitz targeting the youth, so as to encourage the youth to visit the parks.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: When we dig deeper, we realised that the park visitors in the US consist largely of baby-boomers and Gen X.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, the US National Park has identified the lukewarm response from the millenniums as the single largest threat to public support for the country's National Park system.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, NParks is not just facing this trend alone.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: There are three reasons why we want to take this approach.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: One, existing, largely optional outreach efforts to our children will naturally attract those who are already pre-disposed to nature, or to children whose school leaders see the benefit of interacting with nature.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: As much as NParks endeavours, a significant number of children may not have a chance to develop a meaningful bond with nature.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Two, MCCY and MOE are expanding the Outward Bound School (OBS), so as to ensure that all Singaporean youths have a chance to experience OBS.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In the same way, our full-time NSFs have regular interaction with nature in their routine exercises.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: At some point or another, our youths will have a mandated dose of nature.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: However, in both situations, we are setting up nature as adversity to be overcome.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: As such, not all of our youths will end up embracing nature in a positive way.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Three, we have set up our education system to cover the fundamentals in life.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For example, over the years, we have started teaching art, so as to imbue our children with a sense of aesthetics.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And we have always taught our children physical education, so as to develop their motor skills and to teach the benefits of sports.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And recently, we have started emphasising on values, so as to equip our children with the right moral compass in life.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In the same manner, especially since our children are raised as city-dwellers in the digital rage, I believe we must build a deep and intuitive connection between our children and nature.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Some of these parks can be the neighbourhood parks, the national parks or the park connectors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Others can be to iconic national parks, such as Pulau Ubin, Chek Jawa or Sungei Buloh.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: While the regular school trips take place, perhaps NParks can dedicate more resources to have park rangers to introduce the beauty of our animals and flora to our children and to introduce them to our excellent SG BioAtlas and sParks apps.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Not all our children will grow up to be passionate nature-lovers, but, at least, growing up, they will have a chance to understand its beauty.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Next, I would like to talk about funding for NParks.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Over the last few years, I have gradually developed a deeper understanding of what NParks does.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: NParks continues to build more iconic park destinations, such as Gardens by the Bay, Pulau Ubin and HortiPark.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: NParks continues to plant more trees as we build more housing estates and many more trees in forested towns like the upcoming Tengah town.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I have no doubt that NParks will effectively stretch every Government dollar it gets.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Recently, my grassroots members and I were invited to NParks' ground-breaking ceremony at Thomson Natural Park.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We had to hike into the middle of the forest.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And during that short journey, our NParks guides gave us a vivid introduction to the various animals living within the vicinity – the Greater Slow Loris, the Banded Leaf Monkey and the Sundar Pangolin.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: With that, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Members have asked questions that broadly encompass two areas.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: First, the protection of greenery and biodiversity, and, second, the maintenance of such.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, let me try to address some of these questions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Residents can also inform NParks if they see trees being damaged during construction.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But there were several questions about the definition, scope, scale and of how the Marine Park will be protected.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Hence, they are under the jurisdiction of the Act.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These areas are described in Part III of the revised Schedule.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The terrestrial areas of the Marine Park are already protected as public parks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The rules governing these public parks are laid out in the subsidiary legislation of the Parks and Trees Act, namely, the Parks and Trees Regulations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They include prohibitions against littering, causing death or injury to animals and restrictions against fishing or collection of organisms, such as corals, without the approval of the Commissioner of Parks and Recreation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These will include restrictions on diving, movement of vessels and the dropping of anchors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will work closely with our marine conservation community, recreational fishing community, boat operators and other relevant stakeholders to develop these new rules.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh spoke about the concern on the scope of protections offered to Sisters' Islands Marine Park.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As I have said earlier in my speech and as I have just reiterated a moment ago, this Marine Park came into being in 2014.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have taken the last few years, NParks managing our Marine Park, and we have now the confidence to make these amendments, but given ourselves the flexibility to make comprehensive rules – made in consultation with the blue fraternity, the marine conservation fraternity and, indeed, the authors of the Blue Plan ‒ to come up with these rules, together with stakeholders like boat operators and our recreational fishing community.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Darryl David asked if the Marine Park could be developed into a leisure and education destination.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: While Sisters' Islands Marine Park is a marine sanctuary, we also want it to be a living classroom for marine conservation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: NParks set up a public gallery on St John's Island in 2015 as an educational resource for visitors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These facilities will offer the public more opportunities for encounters with marine and terrestrial biodiversity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Small Sister's Island will serve as a dedicated site for marine conservation, promoting species recovery and habitat enhancement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Programmes will be conducted to facilitate visits for schools, institutions and organisations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Indeed, even as we want to confer protection on the Marine Park, make it a sanctuary, we also have to bring people to the Marine Park.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Allow them opportunity to come up close with marine life, so they see how valuable and precious this biodiversity is not only for them, but also for their children and grandchildren.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If you keep them away, if you say, "you can't do this; you can't do that, you can't go to the Marine Park, it's off limits", I am not sure that mindshare and support will be there in the community.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef asked about the criteria for an area to be considered a "marine park" and Mr Louis Ng asked if we could bring the coastal areas of nature reserves and parks under the Parks and Trees Act.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh asked about the scale of Sisters' Islands Marine Park, asking why it does not encompass all the areas covered under the Blue Plan.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The importance of the site as a source of coral larvae for dispersal is another important consideration.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, the Sisters' Islands are important natural refugia for corals, from which larvae are dispersed to enrich other sites in the southern islands.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The suggestion to gazette the Sisters' Islands Marine Park in the Blue Plan was validated by NParks' use of modern technology, such as agent-based modelling.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For those who have interest in this area, please let me know and I will get my colleagues to demonstrate to you what agent-based modelling is.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It shows that the Sisters' Islands and the area that we have gazetted are about the richest source of coral larvae in our southern waters, and, from there, as a source of coral larvae, populating other islands in the area.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, we have to start off with the Sisters' Islands Marine Park.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is a rich haven of marine life, both coastal and sea life.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And we will continue to work with the authors of the Blue Plan.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will continue to work with our marine conservation community, with academics interested in the topic, as well as relevant stakeholders, to identify whether there are other areas that are rich or equally rich in biodiversity and which would need that kind of protection.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In response to Mr Louis Ng's question, NParks' management currently covers the foreshore or intertidal areas at Chek Jawa, Sungei Buloh Wetlands Reserve and Labrador Nature Reserve.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For the other coastal parks, for example, East Coast Park, NParks' management extends up to the high water mark, the high tide mark.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Hence, the areas highlighted by Mr Louis Ng are already protected as nature reserves or public parks under the current Parks and Trees Act and Regulations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Louis Ng also mentioned that NParks has been reporting misdemeanours to Maritime Port Authority (MPA) even though NParks issued a Notice stating that Chek Jawa is protected under the Parks and Trees Act.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: NParks will stop unauthorised activities that it comes across, but will seek the assistance of MPA where it is necessary to supplement its efforts in enforcement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will look into stepping up enforcement at Chek Jawa.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But simply relying on enforcement will not be 100% effective, as no one can be on patrol everywhere and all the time, even though opportunities for technology to come into play are being explored.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In this regard, we will work closely with our environmental community and our Friends of the Park Communities, including a soon-to-be established Friends of the Sisters' Islands Marine Park, and continue to share with the fishing and recreational boating communities on the Dos and Don'ts at Chek Jawa and other coastal areas.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: On this note, I would like to address Mr Louis Ng's query on whether we can restrict the release of animals everywhere, instead of just within the reserves and in watercourses leading to the reserves.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Alex Yam also spoke against the release of animals like terrapins into the wild, into the open.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Indeed, the release of such invasive species has adverse effects on our native ecosystems.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Other less hardy species that are released are unlikely to survive and very often die a slow and painful death.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We can certainly study the feasibility of Mr Louis Ng's suggestion, but, for now, NParks will ramp up public education to increase public awareness about the impact of such behaviour.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Alex Yam also asked about how we would mitigate any negative impact on the Kranji Marshes, or I believe Sungei Buloh, arising from major developments across the Straits.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will certainly protect Sungei Buloh Wetlands Nature Reserve by continuing our efforts in habitat restoration/enhancement and we have a very active Friends of the Sungei Buloh Wetlands Reserve, comprising very passionate members of the nature fraternity and other stakeholders, who help us keep an eye and continue to enhance the richness of Sungei Buloh.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Members also asked about how NParks would be able to distinguish between animals that have strayed and those that have been abandoned and also asked about measures taken to return stray animals to their owners.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: An animal that has been abandoned is one which the owner has deliberately and permanently given up care and control over and typically leaves it in a public place.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: An animal which has strayed is one that has wandered off or is lost, often due to the owner's neglect.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: NParks will investigate and work with agencies like AVA to ascertain if there are any identifying factors, such as microchips, to trace the owners.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: NParks also works with relevant agencies to ensure that the welfare of the animal is not compromised.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef asked if more areas can be designated as heritage roads.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will certainly study the feasibility of doing so.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Next, let me move on to the maintenance of greenery which several Members spoke about.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat suggested that NParks intervene when trees are "inappropriately" located in private homes or when noisy grass-cutting occurs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: He also asked whether residents can contact NParks for issues caused by plants, such as large cacti.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Darryl David, Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef and Er Dr Lee Bee Wah asked what constitutes "danger" from trees.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Such greenery, usually trees, often show signs of structural weakness or poor health.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, they may have severe diseases or pest infestations, or bare crowns with branches overhanging property.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: To determine if the condition of a tree is dangerous, qualified arborists from NParks will use their technical expertise and judgement to assess the tree and its structural integrity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As for noisy grass-cutting, regulation of noise technically comes under NEA.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But NParks does train workers to adhere to appropriate noise protection levels as required by the Workplace Safety and Health regime under MOM.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah also asked if NParks would intervene in other cases of nuisance involving private greenery and remove roadside trees that cause disamenity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For neighbourly disputes arising from nuisance from trees, such as the shedding of leaves, NParks will continue to direct them to existing community dispute resolution channels.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Nparks will only issue advisories to occupiers to prune trees to minimise disamenity, if necessary.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As Mr Darryl David rightfully pointed out, neighbours should try to work things out between themselves first.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
