text: Relying on legal and regulatory action often leads to long-term deep-seated resentment and erodes community bonds.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef asked about the pruning schedules of trees.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The frequency varies according to location, species, age and the condition of the trees.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But it generally ranges between 12 and 24 months.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: That said, there could be higher frequencies of six months in some localities, for instance, where there is heavy pedestrian and vehicular traffic.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Darryl David asked if NParks could manage more public greenery.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: MND, together with NParks, had conducted a centralisation of greenery maintenance exercise last year.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Following this, the greenery in most state lands is now managed by NParks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But some areas are not managed by NParks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, Town Councils are responsible for managing common areas, such as parks, playgrounds and open spaces within public housing estates.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But NParks shares its expertise and provides professional training in plant and maintenance topics for Town Councils or Managing Agents administering landscape contracts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Regardless of which entity is responsible for the greenery, residents can easily report greenery matters through the Municipal Services Office's OneService App.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The feedback will be channelled to the appropriate entity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: NParks works closely with the relevant entities to resolve greenery-related issues.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There were some other points that were raised.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Leon Perera asked about consultation and gave many ideas about how consultation could be weaved into planting programmes and schedules.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I have explained in my Parliamentary Question reply not too long ago that in big projects, like in the Jurong Lake region, but also where there is opportunity to rejuvenate estates, NParks takes the opportunity to consult and get the community involved.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Leon Perera came up with many ideas about consultation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are fully in support of residents and members of the public taking a proactive part, being passionate about things like greenery.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is entirely consonant with our concept of City in a Garden and we will certainly look into how consultation can be enhanced at every stage where possible.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Leon Perera also talked about land reduction at Singapore Botanic Gardens (SBG).

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is due to the MRT station opening at Bukit Timah.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, we took a bit of the frontage to have the opening for the MRT station that brings Singaporeans from around the island to the Singapore Botanic Gardens.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Leon Perera also asked about Auxiliary Police Officers (APOs) and why they are needed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: NParks, as with many agencies, will always have to prioritise manpower.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Manpower is always a challenge, with growing workload and increasing public expectation but tight constraints on manpower.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Deployment of technology – but also maximising manpower by leveraging on trained professionals, such as APOs, such as private security, to help us at the penumbra of regulation, enforcement and monitoring – allows NParks officers to focus and use their deep knowledge in botany and their understanding of the biological sciences to enrich and enhance our parks, nature reserves and so on.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I missed this point: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh asked about whether this new clause in the Bill will be the harbinger of turning of the Marine Park into Disneyland or something like that.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I think that is certainly not at all on the plans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The formation of the Marine Park was not just formed by NParks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It was done in consultation with some of the authors of the Blue Plan and many members of the blue fraternity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I think they will be very distraught to hear any suggestion of that and I hope that Assoc Prof Daniel Goh will explain that this was just a concern and not cause alarm.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In fact, I said earlier that we are looking to form, very shortly, a Friends of the Sisters' Island Marine Park and, just like the Friends of Sungei Buloh Wetlands Reserve, Chestnut Nature Park and elsewhere, we bring together the nature fraternity and those who love arts, music, exercise and sports, all the stakeholders, people who are passionate about our greenery, to come together and to help us energise, activate and programme our parks, including the Marine Park.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But suffice to say that around our nature reserves, we have buffers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In addition to green buffers, we also have established buffer parks, like the soon-to-be-established Thomson Nature Park that Mr Henry Kwek talked about and other buffer parks around nature reserves.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These buffers, as well as buffer parks and nature parks, help to shield the core of the nature reserve from urban life.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They help protect the nature reserve from the desiccating effects of buildings, concrete and traffic.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But they also give NParks the opportunity to go into these buffers to remove alien plant species, conduct animal species surveys and to remove invasive species that have been deliberately or accidentally released from these developments into the nature reserves.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, we share Mr Leon Perera's concern about the integrity of the ecology of our nature reserves.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: A former colleague of mine from NParks coined a new term called the "biophilial" city.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If you look at other countries around the world, big countries with Taman Negara, with national parks, nature reserves, vast areas that they can protect or at least attempt to protect by the letter of the law, the conception is very different.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There you prohibit a whole series of activities and try to tell people, "please do not go there, minimise contact, keep a distance, let nature thrive." In Singapore, we are different.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In other countries, the environment, the greenery and nature envelop cities and their concern is about sprawl, it is about human intervention.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are a City in a Garden where our city envelops our nature reserves, nature parks and our biodiversity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And we have a tremendous amount of biodiversity in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, that is to be celebrated and cherished, and education is critical.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In Singapore, we have to be biophilic and, that means, communities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As stakeholders, we have to be good custodians and stewards of our biodiversity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Not just keeping it away at arms' length through legislation and prohibitions, but to educate, excite and enthuse people about how to care for the plants and animal species that make us a very special place.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, I think that approach should address Mr Leon Perera's concern about what if native animals escape from the nature reserves, what should people do.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I think as custodians and stewards, we need to call NParks, call the necessary authorities, call ACRES, and they will know how to re-introduce the animal, rehabilitate it and bring it back into the wild.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Capturing of wild animals is an offence under the Wild Animals and Birds Act and appropriate action will be taken.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Lastly, I thank Mr Henry Kwek for his encouraging words for NParks officers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Many of them work silently in the background.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They work assiduously and very hard, often behind the scenes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And your encouragement, I think, goes a long way to bring up their spirits.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: NParks works closely with MOE through its Community-in-Nature initiatives, as well as programmes, such as Every Child A Seed and Nature Cares.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Information of our natural heritage has been incorporated into the curriculum, through textbooks and learning journeys to the Singapore Botanic Gardens, our nature reserves and parks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And as suggested by Mr Kwek, we will continue to look at ways to engage the younger generation, including the use of digital platforms to reach out to the increasingly tech-savvy student population.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This includes gamification, augmented reality and push notifications on flora and fauna.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In fact, if you take the time to meet our young conservationists, they are passionate about celebrating, studying and educating others about Singapore's rich biodiversity and our natural heritage.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There is this young man, an undergraduate, Mr Shawn Yap, some of you may have heard about him.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: He used the Pokemon game and the Pokemon craze as an opportunity to excite young people who are normally stuck with their iPhones, to excite them and to show them the beauty of what there is in our reserves and why it is important to protect it.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I would also like to assure Members that NParks is adopting sustainable landscape practices to ensure that our greenery remains maintainable, such as through the use of drought-tolerant native plants.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: NParks is leveraging on technology to enhance productivity, including increased mechanisation in maintenance operations and the use of GIS-enabled mobile devices, for tree inspections.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Alex Yam also voiced concerns on behalf of nursery operators about their leases and about uncertainty of their leases.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: NParks has spent the last three years engaging and visiting nursery operators to understand their needs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But we also recognise that a one-size-fits-all solution may not be applicable to all businesses, including some who have a model that involves more investment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Hence, NParks is also studying the feasibility of leasing selected areas for much longer tenures, for example, 10, plus 10, or some other arrangement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: A recent study by MIT named Singapore as the world's greenest city.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Government, civil society and many members of the public are committed to ensuring that Singapore remains a lush and verdant City in a Garden.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As I have said at the start, we will continually review and update the Act so that our City in a Garden endures.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah, please keep your clarification short.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: Because if they are not successful in tendering, it is very difficult for them to relocate their whole nursery.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Having said that, land is scarce in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Some areas may have to be used for other needs and, therefore, we need to do a comprehensive study and will announce at the appropriate juncture.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: I have two clarifications for the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: One is on scope and one on scale.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: And the first one is that I appreciate that a lot of protection will practically be there but there is also the signalling and symbolic function of legislating the marine park as a nature reserve.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: So, would the Government be open to allowing the management of the marine park to evolve just as Sungei Buloh Wetland Reserve, and to be eventually enshrined legislatively, in law, as a nature reserve in the future?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Are there plans to include the other Southern Islands into the marine park, especially if the marine biodiversity improves precisely because of the existing gazetted marine park?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As I have said earlier, we are but three years into managing a marine park.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It involves protecting different forms of habitats, both terrestrial, intertidal as well as marine.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Putting it into a subsidiary legislation allows us to adjust along the way.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As we encounter new situations, we can amend the legislation in order to quickly confer those protections that are necessary.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As far as signalling is concerned, apart from this legislative amendment, in 2014, we emphasised the importance of the Marine Park, how valuable it is, the publicity, the outreach surrounding it, the developments, the investments on Sisters' Islands and St John's Island to create a living classroom, a research haven and a place for the conservation of marine biodiversity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is a tremendous signal in and of itself and we should celebrate that together.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As for the scale, as I have said earlier, using agent-based modelling but also through the assiduous work of our civil society, nature society and other marine groups, such as Wild Singapore, confirming that the Sisters' Islands Marine Park or the areas that we have gazetted, are the richest in terms of coral larvae.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They are the source, so it has to be protected.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: That does not preclude us ‒ indeed, we are continuing to consult with the nature groups, we are using science and technology – to see whether other areas should also be included as national parks.      .
